title: Diagnosing and Correcting Bias in MLLM for Long Video Understanding

paper.title: Diagnosing and Correcting Bias in MLLM for Long Video Understanding
paper.abstract: Abstract Long-video question answering is challenging since the answer often hinges on a few decisive moments scattered throughout the video, while memory constraints force Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to sample frames at extremely low rates, resulting in sparsity that risks omitting key evidence. Though aggressively enlarging the context size is intuitive, we argue that performance remains fundamentally constrained by the bias, i.e. , the misleading cues caused by spurious linguistic correlations and salient yet irrelevant visual observations. In this paper, we first introduce S-MME, a benchmark designed to systematically diagnose shortcut-biased behavior in MLLMs. To mitigate this failure, we further propose a training-free framework, Counterfactual Long-video Evidence-Aware Reasoning (CLEAR). By treating the full video-question pair as a complete view, CLEAR estimates bias effects via augmented views by only keeping the question or locally salient visual clips. Then, we intervene hidden states to mitigate the discrepancy at inference such that the correct answer can be predicted confidently. With experimental studies across five benchmarks, we show that our method is generalizable and can be integrated in different MLLMs, yielding consistent gains in prediction and robustness. We hope CLEAR can offer a complementary direction in test-time scaling for long-video understanding and will publish code.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Visual understanding over a long temporal horizon is inherently challenging because the correct answer often hinges on a few decisive frames, i.e. , evidence , sparsely dispersed across the video. Then, memory constraints force current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to sample frames at extremely low rates as the input context, further compounding this difficulty and inducing the model to rely on spurious correlations, i.e. , shortcuts , for prediction. To mitigate predictions, the intuitive methods are to scale up the sampling rate and context window [ 49 ] , increase visual token capacity [ 36 ] , and strengthen instruction tuning [ 6 ] . Nevertheless, they all incur substantially higher computational cost and inevitably face an efficiency–effectiveness trade-off. At the same time, enlarging the context alone is insufficient, and performance remains fundamentally constrained by biases even when relevant frames are completely fed into the model. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , the model is prone to follow misleading cues, including (left) spurious linguistic correlations [ 1 ] , where the phrasing of the question and answer options makes a distractor plausible without viewing the video, and (right) salient yet causally irrelevant observations, i.e. , frames that are semantically related to the query yet do not determine the answer. Similarly, while existing methods such as frame selection [ 47 ] , token pruning [ 31 ] and memory mechanisms [ 33 ] , aim to filter out irrelevant frames before feeding them into the model, they still assume that the model can be robust enough to use the key observation. To this end, we believe that evaluation should go beyond aggregate dataset scopes and systematically target samples that are sensitive to shortcuts. Figure 1: MLLMs often fail despite the presence of decisive evidence, either by following spurious linguistic correlations or by over-relying on salient but misleading visual observations. CLEAR diagnoses these shortcut-biased trajectories with controlled probes and steers the full-video representation toward evidence-consistent prediction. In detail, we construct S-MME, standing for Shortcuts in Multi-Modal Evaluation , a long-video benchmark composed of video-question pairs designed to expose shortcut-sensitive failures, i.e. , when given a restricted observation that forces a spurious correlation, models produce an incorrect prediction, whereas access to the evidence frames can yield the correct answer. Then, following the examples in Fig. 1 and adopting the concept of counterfactual samples [ 27 ] , we construct the restricted view in two aspects: a question-only view where the question and options alone make distracted prediction, and a salient-yet-irrelevant view where individual clips have high semantic similarity to the question in a common representation space yet lack the decisive evidence required for the correct answer. In this way, we can directly test whether a model follows the decisive clips or instead collapses to a counterfactual alternative. To further mitigate the bias to such spurious shortcut, we propose a training-free framework Counterfactual Long-video Evidence-Aware Reasoning (CLEAR). CLEAR runs the frozen model, treats the full video-question pair as a complete view, and constructs counterfactual views that maximally preserve the shortcut signals and weaken or even remove decisive evidence. Specifically, we use a question-only view to expose linguistic bias and a salient view formed from highly similar visual observations to expose visual bias. We posit that the prediction discrepancy between views serves as an estimate of the bias effect, and we apply lightweight residual steering in deep layers to intervene on hidden states and suppress spurious correlations, thereby minimizing the distraction and enabling the model to predict the correct answer with more confidence. Meanwhile, our method is generalizable and can be integrated into different MLLMs without additional training, and yields consistent gains through comprehensive experimental studies. Finally, our contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify bias from 1) spurious linguistic correlations and 2) salient but misleading visual observations as a fundamental bottleneck in long-video understanding by MLLMs, which persists beyond sparse frame sampling alone. • To examine such bias of existing MLLMs, we introduce S-MME, a benchmark for systematically diagnosing this behavior. The S-MME considers spurious correlation caused by either linguistic correlation or salient-yet-misleading views. • We propose CLEAR, a training-free framework that estimates bias effects from counterfactual views and mitigates them through hidden-state intervention, thereby encouraging predictions to rely on decisive evidence. The method is generalizable and can be applied to different MLLMs operating in either classification or next-token prediction modes. • Through experimental study, we demonstrate consistent improvements over three public datasets, Video-MME [ 11 ] , LongVideoBench [ 41 ] , and MLVU [ 54 ] , as well as our S-MME benchmark.

sections.heading: Multimodal LLMs for Long-Video Understanding
sections.text: Recent Video-LLMs improve long-video understanding by increasing the amount of visual evidence that can be processed within limited model context. Existing methods typically compress frame-level features into compact visual tokens [ 22 , 56 , 46 , 38 , 20 ] , reduce spatial-temporal redundancy through pooling, token aggregation, or adaptive filtering [ 26 , 45 , 44 , 12 ] , or extend multimodal context length to support more frames and longer reasoning horizons [ 49 , 36 , 35 , 5 , 24 ] . While these methods improve evidence access, often with non-trivial memory or computational cost [ 17 , 32 , 15 , 14 , 13 ] , our work studies a complementary problem: whether accessible evidence is faithfully used when shortcut cues provide plausible answers.

sections.heading: Shortcut Learning and Bias in Visual Question Answering
sections.text: Shortcut learning has long been recognized as a central challenge in visual question answering. Early studies showed that VQA models can exploit answer priors, question templates, or dataset correlations without sufficient visual grounding [ 1 , 3 , 16 , 18 , 29 ] . Subsequent work exposed and mitigated such biases through distribution-shifted benchmarks, language-bias suppression, stronger visual grounding, and counterfactual sample construction [ 1 , 10 , 7 , 27 ] . While these studies provide important insights, they mainly focus on static-image VQA or conventional multimodal fusion. Long-video reasoning introduces an additional shortcut source: a locally salient clip may appear predictive but miss temporally distributed events, state changes, or later evidence required for the correct answer. Recent video QA benchmarks also suggest that final answer accuracy alone does not fully reveal whether models ground their predictions in the relevant temporal evidence [ 43 , 41 , 23 ] . Our work extends shortcut diagnosis from language-only bias to both language-prior and partial-observation shortcuts in long-video reasoning.

sections.heading: Training-Free Methods for Long-Video Understanding
sections.text: Training-free long-video methods improve frozen Video-LLMs through inference-time input selection, memory construction, or agentic reasoning, without updating model parameters [ 19 ] . Selection-based methods reduce redundant visual input through adaptive keyframe sampling, token merging, or query-guided retrieval [ 34 , 50 , 47 , 52 ] . Memory-enhanced methods maintain long-range information using event memory, temporal caches, recursive summarization, or tree-structured video representations [ 33 , 9 , 30 , 40 ] . Agent-based methods formulate long-video QA as an active inference process, iteratively retrieving segments, revising plans, and performing multi-step reasoning with language agents [ 37 , 4 , 53 , 39 , 42 ] . These approaches mainly optimize which evidence is selected, retained, or queried during inference.

sections.heading: 3.1 Making Evidence Use Diagnosable
sections.text: Long-video QA evaluation typically reports whether a model produces the correct answer. However, final-answer accuracy alone does not reveal whether the model has relied on the decisive evidence. A model may fail because the decisive evidence is missing from the sampled context, but it may also fail even when such evidence is available, because the prediction is dominated by shortcut cues such as spurious linguistic correlations or salient-yet-misleading visual observations. We refer to the latter as biased evidence use: the model observes relevant evidence but still follows a plausible shortcut. This behavior is difficult to isolate with long-video benchmarks, where a wrong answer may arise from missing frames, temporal ambiguity, or shortcut-induced bias. To make evidence use diagnosable, we construct cases in which complete video evidence and restricted shortcut cues support competing answers. If a model predicts the shortcut-consistent distractor under the full-video input, the failure indicates that the model does not fully use the decisive evidence. Accordingly, we introduce S-MME, a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating shortcut-robust long-video reasoning.

sections.heading: 3.2 Shortcut-Sensitive Cases
sections.text: The basic unit of S-MME is a shortcut-sensitive long-video QA case. Each case consists of a long video, a question, answer candidates, a sufficient evidence span, and an annotated shortcut-consistent distractor. A valid conflict case must satisfy three conditions. First, the full video contains sufficient evidence to determine a unique correct answer. Second, at least one restricted observation, such as the question alone or a short salient clip, is insufficient for determining the correct answer. Third, this restricted view makes a specific incorrect answer plausible, yielding a shortcut-consistent distractor. We consider two dominant shortcut sources. The first comes from spurious linguistic correlations, where the question or answer options alone make an incorrect answer plausible without visual grounding. The second comes from salient-yet-misleading visual observations, where a visually salient segment is semantically related to the question but does not determine the answer without broader temporal context. These two sources reflect common shortcut pathways in long-video QA and provide counterfactual views for diagnosis. Beyond assigning each case to one shortcut source, S-MME annotates the sufficient evidence span and the shortcut-consistent distractor for every sample. Figure 2: Construction pipeline of S-MME. We first mine candidate questions with explicit long-video evidence requirements, then use restricted views to identify shortcut-consistent distractors, followed by human validation of answer uniqueness, evidence sufficiency, and shortcut plausibility. sections.heading: 3.3 Benchmark Construction
sections.text: We construct S-MME through a three-stage pipeline, as illustrated in Figure 2 . The first stage mines candidate QA samples with explicit long-video evidence requirements. Given a long video, we segment it into coherent temporal events and summarize the timeline with concise event descriptions. Candidate questions are generated from these event summaries to require evidence beyond a single isolated observation, such as cross-event comparison, temporal state change, delayed outcome, or local observation contradicted by later evidence. For each candidate, annotators mark the sufficient evidence span and verify that the full video uniquely determines the correct answer. The second stage uses restricted views to identify shortcut-consistent distractors. For the question-only view, annotators check whether the question and answer options alone make a particular incorrect option plausible without visual grounding. For the salient-view, annotators identify a short segment that is semantically related to the question and supports a plausible distractor, but does not contain sufficient evidence to determine the correct answer without broader video context. These restricted views are used only for candidate discovery and do not determine the ground truth of a sample. The third stage applies human validation and quality control. Annotators retain a candidate only if it satisfies three criteria: (i) the full video uniquely supports the correct answer, (ii) the restricted view is insufficient for determining the correct answer, and (iii) the annotated shortcut-consistent distractor is plausible under the restricted view. Ambiguous questions, multiple-answer cases, noisy videos, and samples without a clearly identifiable evidence span are removed. This meticulous validation pipeline ensures that S-MME evaluates whether models can leverage available evidence to override plausible shortcuts, effectively decoupling reasoning robustness from annotation noise or missing information.

sections.heading: 4.1 Problem Setup
sections.text: We consider a video MLLM parameterized by θ \theta , which takes a video v v and a textual query x x as input, and generates a response y = ( y 1 , … , y T ) y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}) in an auto-regressive manner: y t ∼ p θ ​ ( y t ∣ v , x , y < t ) , y_{t}\sim p_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid v,x,y_{<t}), (1) where y < t y_{<t} denotes previously generated tokens. Long-video understanding requires the model to integrate evidence across temporally distant clips. Errors may still occur when the relevant evidence is present, because the model can form a reasoning trajectory dominated by biases. CLEAR addresses this issue by exposing such shortcut trajectories through counterfactual views and correcting the full-video trajectory through residual steering.

sections.heading: 4.2 Shortcut Probing via Counterfactual Views
sections.text: To make shortcut-biased reasoning observable, CLEAR evaluates the same video-question sample under counterfactual observations. These observations are not used to produce the final answer. Instead, they provide diagnostic trajectories that reveal how the model behaves when complete video evidence is removed or restricted. We focus on two common shortcut sources in long-video reasoning: language priors from the question itself and local visual shortcuts from salient but incomplete clips. Question-only probe. The question-only probe removes the video input and keeps only the textual query. This view captures the model’s spurious linguistic correlations, allowing the model to predict without visual evidence. For questions containing semantic associations or stereotypical object-action relations, the model may assign high probability to a plausible but visually unsupported answer. Salient-view probe. The salient-view probe keeps only a small number of locally relevant clips. sections.text: The counterfactual probes above expose alternative trajectories formed under incomplete observations. CLEAR uses these trajectories as contrastive anchors to correct the full-video reasoning process. The key intuition is that the difference between the full-video trajectory and a shortcut-probe trajectory defines a direction from restricted-view reasoning toward complete-observation reasoning. Shortcut residuals. Given the full-video hidden state 𝐡 l f \mathbf{h}_{l}^{f} and a shortcut-probe hidden state 𝐡 l m \mathbf{h}_{l}^{m} at layer l l , where m ∈ { q , s } m\in\{q,s\} , we define: 𝐫 l m = 𝐡 l f − 𝐡 l m . \mathbf{r}_{l}^{m}=\mathbf{h}_{l}^{f}-\mathbf{h}_{l}^{m}. (5) This residual is not assumed to be a disentangled shortcut component. Instead, it is a directional contrast between incomplete-observation reasoning and full-video reasoning. In other words, it reflects the representational contrast between the restricted-view trajectory and the full-video trajectory. For the two counterfactual probes, 𝐫 l q \mathbf{r}_{l}^{q} provides a correction direction against spurious linguistic correlations, while 𝐫 l s \mathbf{r}_{l}^{s} provides a correction direction against salient-yet-misleading visual observations. Adding activated residuals therefore moves the full-video state away from the shortcut anchors. The remaining decoder layers then continue computation from the corrected state.

sections.heading: Where and when to intervene.
sections.text: Although residual directions can be constructed at every layer, not all layers are equally suitable for correction. Figure 4: Effect of intervention location. Late-layer intervention performs best, with the last block achieving the highest accuracy. We empirically compare intervention at different decoder blocks and find that late-layer intervention is the most effective, with the last block, layers 28–35, giving the best performance, as shown in Figure 4 . This is consistent with the intuition that answer-oriented representations are formed near the decoding stage. Within the selected layers, we further determine when to apply intervention based on the discrepancy between the full-video trajectory and the shortcut-probe trajectory: d l m = 1 − cos ⁡ ( 𝐡 l f , 𝐡 l m ) . d_{l}^{m}=1-\cos(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{f},\mathbf{h}_{l}^{m}). (8) A larger d l m d_{l}^{m} indicates that the shortcut probe induces a more distinct reasoning trajectory. We therefore activate intervention only when d l m > τ d_{l}^{m}>\tau , using a fixed threshold τ = 0.15 \tau=0.15 in all experiments.

sections.heading: Models and Benchmarks.
sections.text: We evaluate CLEAR on representative open-source long-video MLLMs, including LLaVA-Video-7B, InternVL3-8B, and Qwen3-VL-8B. Closed-source models, including GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-Pro, are reported only as reference systems since their hidden states are inaccessible. Experiments are conducted on four public long-video benchmarks, Video-MME, LongVideoBench, LVBench, and MLVU, covering general video QA, long-context temporal reasoning, and complex event-level understanding. We further evaluate on S-MME, our diagnostic benchmark for measuring whether models collapse to shortcut-consistent alternatives.

sections.heading: Compared to open-source baselines.
sections.text: As shown in Table 2 , CLEAR consistently improves open-source long-video MLLMs under the same final-frame budget and decoding setting. The gains are most pronounced on reasoning-intensive benchmarks: CLEAR improves Qwen3-VL-8B by +7.8 on MLVU and +7.2 on Video-MME-Long. For InternVL3-8B, CLEAR improves Video-MME Overall by +3.6, Video-MME Long by +4.2, and LVBench by +6.3. On LLaVA-Video-7B, CLEAR also achieves a clear +5.9 improvement on Video-MME. These results show that CLEAR improves general long-video understanding without increasing the final-frame budget or changing the backbone. The stronger gains on MLVU and Video-MME-Long suggest that standard long-video benchmarks also contain evidence-use failures, where relevant evidence is present but models still rely on shortcut cues. sections.heading: 5.4 Is More Context Enough?
sections.text: A natural way to improve long-video understanding is to sample more frames. We compare the baseline and CLEAR under different frame budgets to test whether context scaling alone resolves shortcut-biased errors. On S-MME, we report both accuracy and ShortErr; on Video-MME, we report accuracy as a representative public benchmark. Figure 5 shows that more frames improve baseline accuracy, confirming the importance of evidence access. However, ShortErr decreases more slowly, indicating that context scaling alone does not fully resolve biased evidence use. Across all frame budgets, CLEAR achieves higher accuracy and lower ShortErr, and its gains on Video-MME suggest that shortcut correction generalizes beyond S-MME. Figure 5: Context scaling analysis. CLEAR consistently improves accuracy and reduces ShortErr under the same frame budget.

sections.heading: 5.5 Do Shortcut Probes Align with Conflict Types?
sections.text: CLEAR uses two restricted views to expose different bias sources: the question-only probe targets spurious linguistic correlations, while the salient-view probe targets salient-yet-misleading visual observations. We compare single-branch and dual-branch variants on S-MME to examine whether these probes play source-specific roles. Table 4 shows that Q-only mainly improves cases dominated by spurious linguistic correlations, indicating its ability to capture question-option priors. S-only is more effective on cases involving salient-yet-misleading visual observations, suggesting that locally plausible visual cues cannot be diagnosed from language alone. Dual-branch variants further improve overall robustness, showing that the two restricted views provide complementary correction signals.

sections.heading: 5.6 Efficiency and Intervention Analysis
sections.text: Although CLEAR introduces auxiliary shortcut probes, its goal is not to simply increase inference compute. We compare it with a direct compute-scaling baseline that uses more full-video frames. Table 5 (a) shows that increasing the full-video context brings limited gains with noticeably higher cost, while CLEAR achieves larger accuracy improvements under comparable inference budgets. This suggests that the benefit mainly comes from shortcut diagnosis and residual corrections. We further study the strength of residual correction. Table 5 (b) shows that a moderate residual scale gives the best accuracy–robustness trade-off. When α \alpha becomes too large, ShortErr continues to decrease slightly, but accuracy starts to drop, indicating over-correction. Overall, CLEAR remains training-free: the backbone is frozen, and the probes only provide inference-time correction signals.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We studied shortcut-driven failures in long-video MLLMs, where models may rely on spurious linguistic correlations or salient yet misleading visual observations despite the presence of decisive evidence. To diagnose this behavior, we introduced S-MME, a benchmark that tests whether models follow complete video evidence or collapse to shortcut-consistent alternatives. We further proposed CLEAR, a training-free inference-time framework that uses counterfactual views to expose shortcut-induced trajectories and applies late-layer residual steering to the full-video path. Experiments on public long-video benchmarks and S-MME show that CLEAR consistently improves accuracy and reduces shortcut-consistent errors across different MLLMs.

sections.heading: A.1 Limitation
sections.text: CLEAR is training-free but not cost-free. Since it uses question-only and salient-view probes to estimate shortcut residuals, each sample requires additional auxiliary forward passes before final full-video decoding. This multi-perspective inference introduces extra latency and computation compared with a vanilla single-pass baseline, particularly for long videos and large MLLM backbones. Our current focus is to validate the effectiveness of controlled shortcut probes for evidence-grounded reasoning. Improving the efficiency of CLEAR is an important future direction. Potential solutions include adaptive probe activation, lightweight probe approximations, representation caching, shared early-layer computation, and early exiting when the discrepancy between the full-video and shortcut-probe trajectories is small.

sections.heading: A.2 Implementation Details
sections.text: All experiments are conducted with frozen open-source MLLMs, including LLaVA-Video-7B, InternVL3-8B, and Qwen3-VL-8B. Closed-source models are only reported as reference systems since their hidden states are inaccessible. Unless otherwise specified, we uniformly sample 64 frames from each video for the final full-video inference path. For CLEAR, we run two auxiliary probes before final decoding: a question-only probe and a salient-view probe. The question-only probe removes all visual inputs, while the salient-view probe selects the top- K K query-relevant clips according to attention scores from query tokens to visual tokens; we use K = 4 K=4 by default. The probes are only used to compute shortcut residuals and never directly generate the final answer. For each view, hidden states are extracted at the same textual decision position. Residual steering is applied to late decoder layers. For Qwen3-VL-8B, we use layers 28–35 by default, and for other backbones we use the corresponding late-layer block with the same relative depth. A probe-specific residual is activated only when d l m = 1 − cos ⁡ ( h l f , h l m ) > τ d_{l}^{m}=1-\cos(h_{l}^{f},h_{l}^{m})>\tau , with τ = 0.15 \tau=0.15 for all experiments. The default residual strength is α = 0.15 \alpha=0.15 , selected from { 0.05 , 0.10 , 0.15 , 0.25 , 0.35 } \{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.25,0.35\} according to the accuracy–shortcut suppression trade-off. All experiments are run on NVIDIA H100 GPUs with batch size one for long-video inference. Efficiency is reported as relative inference time normalized by the vanilla 64-frame baseline of the same backbone, including auxiliary probing, residual construction, and final full-video decoding.

sections.heading: Open-ended video QA.
sections.text: To examine whether CLEAR is limited to multiple-choice prediction, we further evaluate it on VideoEvalPro, an open-ended video question answering benchmark. As shown in Table 6 , CLEAR consistently improves free-form generation across all three backbones, with gains of +1.2, +1.5, and +3.4 points on LLaVA-Video-7B, InternVL3-8B, and Qwen3-VL-8B, respectively. Since VideoEvalPro requires models to generate answers without candidate options, these improvements suggest that CLEAR does not merely calibrate multiple-choice scores, but also steers generation toward more evidence-consistent responses. sections.heading: A.3 Broader Impact
sections.text: CLEAR operates as a training-free inference-time module that steers long-video MLLMs toward evidence-consistent predictions. It may improve reliability in long-form video understanding tasks, but it cannot prevent the base MLLMs from generating erroneous, biased, or harmful responses. Therefore, CLEAR should be viewed as a complementary robustness technique rather than a standalone safety mechanism, especially in high-stakes applications.

Though aggressively enlarging the context size is intuitive, we argue that performance remains fundamentally constrained by the bias, i.e. , the misleading cues caused by spurious linguistic correlations and salient yet irrelevant visual observations. In this paper, we first introduce S-MME, a benchmark designed to systematically diagnose shortcut-biased behavior in MLLMs. To mitigate this failure, we further propose a training-free framework, Counterfactual Long-video Evidence-Aware Reasoning (CLEAR). By treating the full video-question pair as a complete view, CLEAR estimates bias effects via augmented views by only keeping the question or locally salient visual clips. Then, we intervene hidden states to mitigate the discrepancy at inference such that the correct answer can be predicted confidently. With experimental studies across five benchmarks, we show that our method is generalizable and can be integrated in different MLLMs, yielding consistent gains in prediction and robustness. We hope CLEAR can offer a complementary direction in test-time scaling for long-video understanding and will publish code. 1 Introduction Visual understanding over a long temporal horizon is inherently challenging because the correct answer often hinges on a few decisive frames, i.e. , evidence , sparsely dispersed across the video. Then, memory constraints force current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to sample frames at extremely low rates as the input context, further compounding this difficulty and inducing the model to rely on spurious correlations, i.e. , shortcuts , for prediction. To mitigate predictions, the intuitive methods are to scale up the sampling rate and context window [ 49 ] , increase visual token capacity [ 36 ] , and strengthen instruction tuning [ 6 ] . Nevertheless, they all incur substantially higher computational cost and inevitably face an efficiency–effectiveness trade-off. At the same time, enlarging the context alone is insufficient, and performance remains fundamentally constrained by biases even when relevant frames are completely fed into the model. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , the model is prone to follow misleading cues, including (left) spurious linguistic correlations [ 1 ] , where the phrasing of the question and answer options makes a distractor plausible without viewing the video, and (right) salient yet causally irrelevant observations, i.e. , frames that are semantically related to the query yet do not determine the answer. Similarly, while existing methods such as frame selection [ 47 ] , token pruning [ 31 ] and memory mechanisms [ 33 ] , aim to filter out irrelevant frames before feeding them into the model, they still assume that the model can be robust enough to use the key observation. To this end, we believe that evaluation should go beyond aggregate dataset scopes and systematically target samples that are sensitive to shortcuts. Figure 1: MLLMs often fail despite the presence of decisive evidence, either by following spurious linguistic correlations or by over-relying on salient but misleading visual observations. CLEAR diagnoses these shortcut-biased trajectories with controlled probes and steers the full-video representation toward evidence-consistent prediction. In detail, we construct S-MME, standing for Shortcuts in Multi-Modal Evaluation , a long-video benchmark composed of video-question pairs designed to expose shortcut-sensitive failures, i.e. , when given a restricted observation that forces a spurious correlation, models produce an incorrect prediction, whereas access to the evidence frames can yield the correct answer. Then, following the examples in Fig. 1 and adopting the concept of counterfactual samples [ 27 ] , we construct the restricted view in two aspects: a question-only view where the question and options alone make distracted prediction, and a salient-yet-irrelevant view where individual clips have high semantic similarity to the question in a common representation space yet lack the decisive evidence required for the correct answer. In this way, we can directly test whether a model follows the decisive clips or instead collapses to a counterfactual alternative. To further mitigate the bias to such spurious shortcut, we propose a training-free framework Counterfactual Long-video Evidence-Aware Reasoning (CLEAR). CLEAR runs the frozen model, treats the full video-question pair as a complete view, and constructs counterfactual views that maximally preserve the shortcut signals and weaken or even remove decisive evidence. Specifically, we use a question-only view to expose linguistic bias and a salient view formed from highly similar visual observations to expose visual bias. We posit that the prediction discrepancy between views serves as an estimate of the bias effect, and we apply lightweight residual steering in deep layers to intervene on hidden states and suppress spurious correlations, thereby minimizing the distraction and enabling the model to predict the correct answer with more confidence. Meanwhile, our method is generalizable and can be integrated into different MLLMs without additional training, and yields consistent gains through comprehensive experimental studies. Finally, our contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify bias from 1) spurious linguistic correlations and 2) salient but misleading visual observations as a fundamental bottleneck in long-video understanding by MLLMs, which persists beyond sparse frame sampling alone. • To examine such bias of existing MLLMs, we introduce S-MME, a benchmark for systematically diagnosing this behavior. The S-MME considers spurious correlation caused by either linguistic correlation or salient-yet-misleading views. • We propose CLEAR, a training-free framework that estimates bias effects from counterfactual views and mitigates them through hidden-state intervention, thereby encouraging predictions to rely on decisive evidence. The method is generalizable and can be applied to different MLLMs operating in either classification or next-token prediction modes. • Through experimental study, we demonstrate consistent improvements over three public datasets, Video-MME [ 11 ] , LongVideoBench [ 41 ] , and MLVU [ 54 ] , as well as our S-MME benchmark. 2 Related Works Multimodal LLMs for Long-Video Understanding Recent Video-LLMs improve long-video understanding by increasing the amount of visual evidence that can be processed within limited model context. Existing methods typically compress frame-level features into compact visual tokens [ 22 , 56 , 46 , 38 , 20 ] , reduce spatial-temporal redundancy through pooling, token aggregation, or adaptive filtering [ 26 , 45 , 44 , 12 ] , or extend multimodal context length to support more frames and longer reasoning horizons [ 49 , 36 , 35 , 5 , 24 ] . While these methods improve evidence access, often with non-trivial memory or computational cost [ 17 , 32 , 15 , 14 , 13 ] , our work studies a complementary problem: whether accessible evidence is faithfully used when shortcut cues provide plausible answers. Shortcut Learning and Bias in Visual Question Answering Shortcut learning has long been recognized as a central challenge in visual question answering. Early studies showed that VQA models can exploit answer priors, question templates, or dataset correlations without sufficient visual grounding [ 1 , 3 , 16 , 18 , 29 ] . Subsequent work exposed and mitigated such biases through distribution-shifted benchmarks, language-bias suppression, stronger visual grounding, and counterfactual sample construction [ 1 , 10 , 7 , 27 ] . While these studies provide important insights, they mainly focus on static-image VQA or conventional multimodal fusion. Long-video reasoning introduces an additional shortcut source: a locally salient clip may appear predictive but miss temporally distributed events, state changes, or later evidence required for the correct answer. Recent video QA benchmarks also suggest that final answer accuracy alone does not fully reveal whether models ground their predictions in the relevant temporal evidence [ 43 , 41 , 23 ] . Our work extends shortcut diagnosis from language-only bias to both language-prior and partial-observation shortcuts in long-video reasoning. Training-Free Methods for Long-Video Understanding Training-free long-video methods improve frozen Video-LLMs through inference-time input selection, memory construction, or agentic reasoning, without updating model parameters [ 19 ] . Selection-based methods reduce redundant visual input through adaptive keyframe sampling, token merging, or query-guided retrieval [ 34 , 50 , 47 , 52 ] . Memory-enhanced methods maintain long-range information using event memory, temporal caches, recursive summarization, or tree-structured video representations [ 33 , 9 , 30 , 40 ] . Agent-based methods formulate long-video QA as an active inference process, iteratively retrieving segments, revising plans, and performing multi-step reasoning with language agents [ 37 , 4 , 53 , 39 , 42 ] . These approaches mainly optimize which evidence is selected, retained, or queried during inference. 3 S-MME: Shortcuts in Multi-Modal Evaluation 3.1 Making Evidence Use Diagnosable Long-video QA evaluation typically reports whether a model produces the correct answer. However, final-answer accuracy alone does not reveal whether the model has relied on the decisive evidence. A model may fail because the decisive evidence is missing from the sampled context, but it may also fail even when such evidence is available, because the prediction is dominated by shortcut cues such as spurious linguistic correlations or salient-yet-misleading visual observations. We refer to the latter as biased evidence use: the model observes relevant evidence but still follows a plausible shortcut. This behavior is difficult to isolate with long-video benchmarks, where a wrong answer may arise from missing frames, temporal ambiguity, or shortcut-induced bias. To make evidence use diagnosable, we construct cases in which complete video evidence and restricted shortcut cues support competing answers. If a model predicts the shortcut-consistent distractor under the full-video input, the failure indicates that the model does not fully use the decisive evidence. Accordingly, we introduce S-MME, a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating shortcut-robust long-video reasoning. 3.2 Shortcut-Sensitive Cases The basic unit of S-MME is a shortcut-sensitive long-video QA case. Each case consists of a long video, a question, answer candidates, a sufficient evidence span, and an annotated shortcut-consistent distractor. A valid conflict case must satisfy three conditions. First, the full video contains sufficient evidence to determine a unique correct answer. Second, at least one restricted observation, such as the question alone or a short salient clip, is insufficient for determining the correct answer. Third, this restricted view makes a specific incorrect answer plausible, yielding a shortcut-consistent distractor. We consider two dominant shortcut sources. The first comes from spurious linguistic correlations, where the question or answer options alone make an incorrect answer plausible without visual grounding. The second comes from salient-yet-misleading visual observations, where a visually salient segment is semantically related to the question but does not determine the answer without broader temporal context. These two sources reflect common shortcut pathways in long-video QA and provide counterfactual views for diagnosis. Beyond assigning each case to one shortcut source, S-MME annotates the sufficient evidence span and the shortcut-consistent distractor for every sample. Figure 2: Construction pipeline of S-MME. The first stage mines candidate QA samples with explicit long-video evidence requirements. Given a long video, we segment it into coherent temporal events and summarize the timeline with concise event descriptions. Candidate questions are generated from these event summaries to require evidence beyond a single isolated observation, such as cross-event comparison, temporal state change, delayed outcome, or local observation contradicted by later evidence. For each candidate, annotators mark the sufficient evidence span and verify that the full video uniquely determines the correct answer. The second stage uses restricted views to identify shortcut-consistent distractors. For the question-only view, annotators check whether the question and answer options alone make a particular incorrect option plausible without visual grounding. For the salient-view, annotators identify a short segment that is semantically related to the question and supports a plausible distractor, but does not contain sufficient evidence to determine the correct answer without broader video context. These restricted views are used only for candidate discovery and do not determine the ground truth of a sample. The third stage applies human validation and quality control. Annotators retain a candidate only if it satisfies three criteria: (i) the full video uniquely supports the correct answer, (ii) the restricted view is insufficient for determining the correct answer, and (iii) the annotated shortcut-consistent distractor is plausible under the restricted view. Ambiguous questions, multiple-answer cases, noisy videos, and samples without a clearly identifiable evidence span are removed. This meticulous validation pipeline ensures that S-MME evaluates whether models can leverage available evidence to override plausible shortcuts, effectively decoupling reasoning robustness from annotation noise or missing information. 4 CLEAR: Counterfactual Long-video Evidence-Aware Reasoning Figure 3: Overview of CLEAR. A natural way to improve long-video understanding is to sample more frames. We compare the baseline and CLEAR under different frame budgets to test whether context scaling alone resolves shortcut-biased errors. On S-MME, we report both accuracy and ShortErr; on Video-MME, we report accuracy as a representative public benchmark. Figure 5 shows that more frames improve baseline accuracy, confirming the importance of evidence access. However, ShortErr decreases more slowly, indicating that context scaling alone does not fully resolve biased evidence use. Across all frame budgets, CLEAR achieves higher accuracy and lower ShortErr, and its gains on Video-MME suggest that shortcut correction generalizes beyond S-MME. Figure 5: Context scaling analysis. CLEAR consistently improves accuracy and reduces ShortErr under the same frame budget. 5.5 Do Shortcut Probes Align with Conflict Types? CLEAR uses two restricted views to expose different bias sources: the question-only probe targets spurious linguistic correlations, while the salient-view probe targets salient-yet-misleading visual observations. We compare single-branch and dual-branch variants on S-MME to examine whether these probes play source-specific roles. Table 4 shows that Q-only mainly improves cases dominated by spurious linguistic correlations, indicating its ability to capture question-option priors. S-only is more effective on cases involving salient-yet-misleading visual observations, suggesting that locally plausible visual cues cannot be diagnosed from language alone. Dual-branch variants further improve overall robustness, showing that the two restricted views provide complementary correction signals. 5.6 Efficiency and Intervention Analysis Although CLEAR introduces auxiliary shortcut probes, its goal is not to simply increase inference compute. We compare it with a direct compute-scaling baseline that uses more full-video frames. Table 5 (a) shows that increasing the full-video context brings limited gains with noticeably higher cost, while CLEAR achieves larger accuracy improvements under comparable inference budgets. This suggests that the benefit mainly comes from shortcut diagnosis and residual corrections. We further study the strength of residual correction. Table 5 (b) shows that a moderate residual scale gives the best accuracy–robustness trade-off. When α \alpha becomes too large, ShortErr continues to decrease slightly, but accuracy starts to drop, indicating over-correction. Overall, CLEAR remains training-free: the backbone is frozen, and the probes only provide inference-time correction signals. 6 Conclusion We studied shortcut-driven failures in long-video MLLMs, where models may rely on spurious linguistic correlations or salient yet misleading visual observations despite the presence of decisive evidence. To diagnose this behavior, we introduced S-MME, a benchmark that tests whether models follow complete video evidence or collapse to shortcut-consistent alternatives. We further proposed CLEAR, a training-free inference-time framework that uses counterfactual views to expose shortcut-induced trajectories and applies late-layer residual steering to the full-video path. Experiments on public long-video benchmarks and S-MME show that CLEAR consistently improves accuracy and reduces shortcut-consistent errors across different MLLMs. Acknowledgments Jiawei Ma acknowledges the support of the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) under Grant No. 62172439 and the Hong Kong Research Grants Council (RGC) under Grant No. TRS T43-101/26-N.
